title: The Mixing Room
intro: New zone. Nothing on this mountain is pure — almost everything is a mixture.

blocks.html:
High on the mountain, grip is everything. The expedition mixes its own grip paste in a back room of base camp, and the recipe is written like this:

chalk : resin = 2 : 3

Read it out loud as two parts chalk to three parts resin. That is a ratio.

Here is the thing worth getting straight before anything else. A part is not a gram. A part is whatever scoop you decide to use — a teaspoon, a mug, a shovel. The ratio only tells you how many scoops of each. It says nothing about how big the scoop is.

One rule, and it is the whole idea: the same scoop for both.

blocks.prompt: The mixer uses a 10 gram scoop, and follows the recipe exactly: 2 parts chalk to 3 parts resin.
blocks.hint: Two scoops of chalk, three of resin. Each scoop weighs 10 grams.

parts.label: Chalk (grams)
parts._working: 2 parts, 10 g per part: 2 × 10 = 20 g of chalk.

parts.label: Resin (grams)
parts._working: 3 parts, 10 g per part: 3 × 10 = 30 g of resin. Sanity check on the pair: 20 g to 30 g, which is 2 : 3 as required.

blocks.prompt: Same recipe, no scales — he is counting scoops straight into the bowl.
blocks.hint: For every 2 scoops of chalk he owes 3 scoops of resin. Work out how many 2s make the chalk, then pay the resin.

parts.label: 4 scoops of chalk needs how many scoops of resin?
parts._working: 4 scoops of chalk is 2 lots of the 2-part chalk share, so the resin is also doubled: 2 × 3 = 6 scoops.

parts.label: 10 scoops of chalk needs how many scoops of resin?
parts._working: 10 scoops of chalk is 5 lots of 2, so the resin is 5 lots of 3: 5 × 3 = 15 scoops. Check: 10 : 15 divides by 5 down to 2 : 3.

blocks.button: Why these are all the SAME paste ✨
blocks.html:
Look at the four batches you have now made, side by side.

BatchChalkResin
One batch23
Double batch46
Triple batch69
Five batches1015

Every single one of those grips exactly the same. A climber could not tell them apart.

That is the surprise, and it is worth saying slowly: multiplying both parts by the same number changes how much paste you have, and it does not change what the paste is.

Which means the arithmetic runs backwards too. If you can divide both parts by the same number, the mixture is unchanged and the recipe gets simpler. 10 : 15 both divide by 5, so 10 : 15 is 2 : 3. That is called putting a ratio in its simplest form, and it is the common-factor hunt you already do with fractions, wearing a different coat.

blocks.prompt: Three batches came back from the store with no labels. Put each recipe into its simplest form. (Type it like 2:3.)
blocks.hint: Hunt for a number that divides into BOTH parts, then divide both by it. Keep going until nothing divides them both.

parts._working: 12 and 18 share a factor of 6: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3, giving 2 : 3. Nothing divides 2 and 3 together, so it is simplest. (Dividing by 2 first gives 6 : 9, then by 3 gives 2 : 3 — same destination, which is worth him noticing.)
9 and 21 share a factor of 3: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 and 21 ÷ 3 = 7, giving 3 : 7. Nothing divides 3 and 7 together. Deliberately NOT a 2 : 3 answer, so the pattern of the previous part cannot be copied blindly.

25 and 20 share a factor of 5: 25 ÷ 5 = 5 and 20 ÷ 5 = 4, giving 5 : 4. Note the bigger number comes FIRST here — the order of a ratio carries meaning, and this part exists to catch anyone who has started assuming the small one leads.

blocks.html:
Now the job that actually comes up at base camp. You are not told the scoop size — you are told the total.

Make 40 scoops of paste, at 2 parts chalk to 3 parts resin.

Three moves, in this order, every time:

1. Count the parts. 2 + 3 = 5 parts altogether.
2. Find ONE part. 40 ÷ 5 = 8 scoops per part.
3. Pay out each share. Chalk is 2 parts: 2 × 8 = 16. Resin is 3 parts: 3 × 8 = 24.

Always check by adding the shares back up: 16 + 24 = 40 ✓.

Remember move 2. Finding one part is the handle this whole unit turns on.

blocks.prompt: The stove fuel is mixed 1 part additive to 5 parts paraffin, and the tank holds 60 litres.
blocks.hint: Count the parts first: 1 + 5. Then divide the 60 by that to find one part.

parts.label: Additive (litres)
parts._working: Parts: 1 + 5 = 6. One part: 60 ÷ 6 = 10. The additive is 1 part, so 10 litres.

parts.label: Paraffin (litres)
parts._working: The paraffin is 5 parts: 5 × 10 = 50 litres. Check: 10 + 50 = 60 ✓, and 10 : 50 divides by 10 down to 1 : 5 ✓.

blocks.prompt: Boss mix. The winter paste takes a third ingredient — grit, for ice. The recipe is 2 parts chalk, 3 parts resin, 5 parts grit, and the mixer needs 200 grams of it.
blocks.hint: Exactly the same three moves, just with one more share to pay out. Count all three parts first.

parts.label: Chalk (grams)
parts._working: Parts: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10. One part: 200 ÷ 10 = 20 g. Chalk is 2 parts: 2 × 20 = 40 g.

parts.label: Grit (grams)
parts._working: Grit is 5 parts: 5 × 20 = 100 g. Check all three against the total: 40 + 60 + 100 = 200 ✓. Worth noticing that grit is 5 of the 10 parts, so it is exactly half the tub.

blocks.prompt: ★ Nobody wrote down the batch size. All you know is the recipe — 3 parts chalk to 4 parts resin — and that the mixer tipped in 18 grams of chalk.
blocks.hint: You are told what 3 parts weighs. So what does ONE part weigh? Everything else follows from that.

parts.label: Resin (grams)
parts._working: 3 parts is 18 g, so one part is 18 ÷ 3 = 6 g. Resin is 4 parts: 4 × 6 = 24 g.

parts.label: Whole batch (grams)
parts._working: Either add the shares, 18 + 24 = 42 g, or count parts first: 3 + 4 = 7 parts at 6 g each, 7 × 6 = 42 g. Both routes agreeing is the check. This is the three moves run in a different order — one part found from a share instead of from the total — and that reversal is the whole of next session, so a nudge here is enough.

blocks.html:
🏔️ For the dinner table: three tubs come back from the store, labelled only with their recipes.

Tub A is 6 : 9. Tub B is 4 : 6. Tub C is 4 : 7.

Two of those tubs hold exactly the same paste. One is an impostor. Which — and how would you convince Dad, with no calculator and no scales?

Then the sting in the tail. The impostor is close to the others, so here is the real question: is it chalkier or resinier than the proper mix? Argue it out. (Careful — the bigger number in the ratio is not automatically the answer.)

done.title: Mix sorted ✓
done.html:
Ratios, from scratch: parts instead of amounts, the same scoop for both, equivalent recipes that look different and grip identically, simplest form by hunting common factors — and the three moves that split any total into any ratio, including a three-way split.

And right at the end, in the ★, you turned the handle the other way: given one share, you found everything else.

Next: Scaling the Recipe — where finding one part stops being a step and becomes the tool.
